A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FLIP segmentation work. Their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison, including matching material relocated from v2's main text into v3's Appendices A–F.

before.justification: v2 reports original segmentation accuracy, runtime measurements, architectural ablations and object-scale analyses across six evaluation datasets.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and reports additional fine-tuned models, baseline comparisons and prompt-noise experiments in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: v3 adds FLIPbb variants that convert boxes into Gaussian prompts, undergo prompt-specific fine-tuning and restrict mask queries to the supplied box. It also adds augmentation-free final fine-tuning for Gaussian-prompt variants. These extend the procedure while retaining the foveated encoder, pixel predictor, sparse BCE loss and hierarchical inference.

E1.justification: SA-1B training and evaluation on Hypersim, KITTI-360, OpenImages, COCO, LVIS and ObjaScale remain. New noisy-box tests expand input-condition coverage to localization errors. The fuller description of ObjaScale's centered target clarifies existing data rather than establishing a changed dataset.

E2.justification: v3 adds SAM2-T, SAM2-S, SAM2-B+ and SAM2-L to the overall and small-object comparisons, and STT-H to the ObjaScale heatmaps in Figure 7. The earlier SAM, EfficientSAM, MobileSAM and FastSAM comparators remain. This substantially strengthens coverage of competing segmentation and foveated methods.

E3.justification: v3 introduces final fine-tuning without augmentation, fixing N=512, coverage=1.44 and overlap threshold=2.67. It adds matched box-information evaluations and a controlled noise protocol using shared instance subsets, corresponding clean controls, box-center/size perturbations and dataset-balanced averages. These are substantive additions to training and evaluation settings.

E4.justification: v3 adds systematic prompt-robustness tests at 2.5%, 5%, 10% and 20% box noise, with per-dataset breakdowns in Appendix C, exposing dependence on localization accuracy. Figure 8 also illustrates sampling sensitivity to coverage, overlap and patch budget. The original architectural ablation results remain unchanged in Table 9.

E5.justification: v3 newly states that noisy evaluations are averaged over repeated perturbations, without giving repetition counts or seeds. It also clarifies that the main tables' standard deviations describe per-instance IoU variability. Existing mean-and-standard-deviation reporting remains; no confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: v3's fine-tuned headline means are 79.90% for FLIP-Tiny and 83.26% for FLIP-Large, versus 78.24% and 80.33% in v2. The original overall results remain unchanged in v3 Table 10, so these are different training conditions. New box-prompt, SAM2 and noise results substantially expand the evidence; Table 2 shows FLIPbb-Large dropping from 79.53% clean to 26.34% at 20% noise. The original small-object hierarchical rows are replaced.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.3 newly defines the box-derived Gaussian using the box midpoint, diagonal covariance, and standard deviations of 0.188 times width and 0.34 times height. The existing attention, predictor, loss and hierarchical-refinement mathematics are retained, largely in Appendices A and F. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central contributions—foveated segmentation, parameter efficiency and scale invariance—remain. v3 explicitly extends superiority claims to SAM2 and qualifies practical applicability through dependence on accurate prompts, while retaining the broader foundation-model ambition.

C2.justification: v3 explains the extra shape/orientation information in mask-derived Gaussians and limits ObjaScale's interpretation to a controlled, single-target scale diagnostic. It attributes noise failures to the prompt controlling both sampled patches and queried pixels, and adds deployment and prompt-interface limitations. These substantially qualify v2's broader performance and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Section 3.1 substantially expand sampler documentation with boundary rejection, a 10Ni attempt limit, retention of underfilled patch buffers and coordinate normalization. v3 also specifies box-to-Gaussian constants and final fine-tuning sampling settings. These disclosures improve reproducibility without establishing that the original sampler itself changed.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning around SAM2, MaskFormer/Mask2Former, DAT, recent foveated backbones and especially STT. It distinguishes STT's fixed point-centered tokenization from FLIP's object-conditioned sampling and explicitly positions FLIP as complementary to object-discovery models, refining the novelty and task relationship described in v2.

P1.justification: v3 reorganizes detailed architecture mathematics, small-object analysis, architectural ablations, cross-dataset discussion and hierarchical inference into appendices. Main-text method descriptions are condensed, sampling explanations expanded, and results and conclusion rewritten around prompt types and robustness. An impact statement is also added.

P2.justification: Figure 7 expands from five to eight heatmaps; new Figures 5 and 8 illustrate sampling behavior. v2's separate attention and predictor diagrams are combined into v3 Figure 9 with an added standard-attention panel. Performance plots and tables are expanded, noise tables added, and numerous displays relocated between main text and appendices.

improvement.justification: v2's central comparisons leave unequal prompt information and sensitivity to inaccurate localization insufficiently examined. v3 addresses these deficiencies through matched box-prompt comparisons and controlled noise tests, while explaining the richer Gaussian prompts and ObjaScale's diagnostic limits. This substantially improves evidential validity and practical interpretation. Fine-tuning budgets and perturbation repetition counts remain incompletely documented, but do not outweigh these gains.
